placement.position_note: PLACED 2026-08-11. THE CORNER IS DOCUMENTED TWICE AND THE COORDINATE IS DERIVED, so the tag follows the weaker half — the rule the Sauganash and Green Tree placements use. Wau-Bun: 'It stood at what is now the southwest corner of Wolcott and N. Water Streets.' Andreas, independently: 'the agency-house on the north side of the river, near where now is the foot of North State Street', with his footnote citing Wau-Bun for the same corner. METHOD, in three steps. (1) Wolcott Street is today's N State Street; its modern centreline was read from OpenStreetMap through the Kinzie intersection (EPSG:26916 E 447899.73, N 4637671.53, local E +827.0, N +275.7) and carried south on the fitted bearing of the OSM centreline, giving E +830 at this northing and a west kerb 12.2 m west of it, half an 80 ft platted street. (2) North Water Street and the 1834 north bank were read off the Wright 1834 sheet at the project's own fitted affine (tools/wright_px.py, the same transform tools/rederive_datum.py checks the datum against): the north-bank block row's south line, which is North Water Street's north kerb, runs at local N +128 to +132 between E +624 and E +812, and the drawn north bank of the main stem runs at local N +98 over the same stretch. So the platted street occupies a strip about 30 m deep between the block row and the water. (3) The building's south face is set 15 m north of that bank line and its east face 4 m west of the State Street kerb. THE 15 M IS EVIDENCE, NOT A GUESS, AND IT IS SOFT: Andreas prints the testimony of Charles Jouett's daughter, Mrs. Susan M. Callis, who came here in 1816 and describes the agency house of that period as 'a log building of two large rooms, about twenty steps from the river bank, on the north side'. Twenty steps is 15-18 m. Two inferences ride on it — that a step is about three-quarters of a metre, and that the house Mrs. Callis describes is the one Wolcott finished, which Andreas's 'commenced during Judge Jouett's incumbency' supports and nobody states. WHAT THE SOUTH-WEST QUADRANT ACTUALLY IS: on the 1834 sheet there is no block in it. West of Wolcott the ground south of North Water Street is the riverbank itself, so the building sits on the bank between the platted street and the water rather than on a corner lot — which is what Wau-Bun describes from the other side: 'when, in the process of the town's improvement, a street was maliciously opened directly in the rear of the building, the whole establishment, with its comical little adjuncts, was a constant source of amusement to the passers-by.' The house predates the plat by a decade and the street was laid out behind it. That same sentence is the evidence for the facade bearing recorded here, 180, due south onto the river: the street opened at the REAR, so the front faced the water, which is also how the fort's people reached it — Wau-Bun has the intercourse between the garrison and the Agency House kept up by canoe. UNCERTAINTY: about 20 m from the georeference (data/datum.json records ~17.5 m RMS and calls 20 m the working figure), plus the reading of the 1834 sheet by eye at about 5 m, plus whatever 'twenty steps' is worth. Treat the across-bank axis as the softer one. A LARGER CAVEAT THAN ALL OF THOSE, AND IT IS DISCHARGED. When this note was written the building stood about 500 m east of the modelled terrain box and there was no modelled ground under it at all. The e1834_harbor_cut heightfield was extended east on 2026-08-11 to local E -320..+1700, N -400..+400 — docs/LIBERTIES.md L17 is revised to say so — and this position has stood on traced ground at about +1.35 m above the summer-1835 water surface ever since, which is why this phase carries no ground_contact declaration. Corrected 2026-08-22 under T-0010; walked in the real page by tools/measure_east_band.mjs.
placement.symbolic_location: South-west corner of Wolcott Street and North Water Street (today N State St and the north bank of the main stem), at the foot of State Street, north bank of the main stem east of the forks.

placement.position_note:
RE-SEATED 2026-10-22 ON THE OWNER'S REPORT (T-3029): 5.80 m WEST, the northing and bearing unchanged. The owner, in the 1835 scene: "green tree tavern in 1835 is sunken, it needs to be on the ground". It was: the renderer beds a building on the lowest ground under it, and the T-0141 seat below was measured on the footprint polygon alone, while the rear ell (form.rear_ell, built since T-0083 off the east gable) runs 4.5 m further down the bank, its far corner 1.54 m from the traced waterline. Bedded to the ell's foot, the inn stood 0.58 m under its own front door; bedded to its bounding box, as the renderer then did, 0.88 m. The rule is the T-0141 rule with the whole building in it: walked west a tenth of a metre at a time, this is the first seat at which every wall foot the mesh puts on the ground, ell included, meets the modelled ground within 0.10 m, the relief 95% of the 1835 town's structures stand on. Here it is 0.099 m, and the ell's far corner stands 4.59 m from the bank. The move is inside the 20 m working uncertainty below and argues nothing new about the corner: the source still puts the inn at Lake and West Water, and the bank still decides how close to it the inn can come. The paragraphs below are the T-0141 seat as it was measured, kept as the reading this one corrects.

MOVED 2026-09-24 ON THE OWNER'S RULING OF 2026-09-21 (T-0141): from the north-east corner of Lake and Canal to the north-east corner of Lake and West Water, 116.40 m east, measured between the old east face and the new one. The northing did not change at all. THE MOVE IS ARGUED FROM THE SOURCE AND NOT FROM A PICTURE'S FRAMING. DRLOIH's article on this tavern gives the corner as 'Lake and West Water Streets'; West Water was the street that ran along the west bank while Canal lay a full plat module further west, and the owner ruled that statement preferred over the same article's gloss 'now Canal Street'. The ship masts that read beside and beyond the inn rather than above its own roofline from the `green_tree` stand (T-0122, T-0140) are the SYMPTOM that sent somebody to look at the placement; they are not a reason to move a building.

WHAT THE OLD PLACEMENT WAS, because a committed building that moves without its previous reading surviving is a town quietly rewriting itself. PLACED 2026-08-09 at EPSG:26916 E 446937.4, N 4637299.6, facade bearing 270: the west face on Canal Street's east frontage and the south face on Lake's north frontage, each half an 80 ft platted street from the modern Lake-and-Canal intersection centre read from OpenStreetMap (E 446913.0, N 4637287.4). That reading rested on chicagology's 'Northeast Corner of Lake and Canal Streets' and on DRLOIH's own body text, 'the N.E. corner of what is now Lake and Canal Streets' — both name Canal in modern terms and one says 'what is now', which is why Canal was adopted at the time. The residual was recorded then and is the thing the ruling settled: modern Canal at Lake stands about 146 m back from the modern west-bank line, so the two readings are a full plat module apart. The check that would settle it from paper is still the lot geometry on Wright 1834 or Hathaway 1834, which nobody has read.

HOW THE NEW COORDINATE IS ARRIVED AT — two constraints, one of them recomputed by tools/validate.py. (1) NORTH OF LAKE, unchanged: the south face stands 12.192 m north of the Lake-and-Canal control's northing, half the 80 ft platted module, which is the `platted_corner` derivation below and keeps the building out of Lake's platted corridor. (2) THE RIVER END: the footprint's north-east corner stands 3.01 m from the 1834 traced west bank of the South Branch (data/terrain/epochs/e1834_harbor_cut/river.geojson) — 5.71 m measured due east at that corner's own northing — and the standoff is the MODELLED GROUND'S OWN LIMIT rather than a chosen setback. The bank falls away toward the water, and a 12.19 m sill plate cannot sit level across that fall: seated hard on the bank the footprint's perimeter stands 0.88 m off the terrain beneath it, which is a building arriving nowhere and would owe a liberty. Walked west a tenth of a metre at a time, the first seat whose whole perimeter comes within the walker's 0.35 m step-up of the modelled ground is this one, at 0.294 m, with the footprint dry at all 425 samples of a 24-by-16 grid over it. So the tavern comes forward to the bank as far as the committed ground carries it, which is what 'forward to the bank' can mean here. Facade bearing is UNCHANGED at 270, due west onto West Water: F. H. Taylor's 'The fornt was on Canal street and this side was on Lake' is a claim about the street the front faced, and on the ruling's reading that street is West Water; the long elevation still runs east-west along Lake, and John Gray's second entrance is still 'on the Lake street front about the middle of the long side'. Working uncertainty about 20 m, which is the georeference's and the traced bank's and not an additional guess.

WHAT THE MOVE DISPLACED, AND ON WHOSE RULE. The committed `west_water` centreline ran through this footprint. T-0768 carried the bank offset 37.12 m past the Wolf Point turn under a stated rule — carry it until the riverward corridor reaches a committed footprint that stands ACROSS the roadway rather than beside it, and cut the line there — and the Green Tree is now the first such footprint, its nearest corner 3.01 m from the bank and its furthest 15.90 m, so it stands across the roadway exactly as James Kinzie's house does. So the line is cut at local [-20.32, -98.49]: 22.53 m shorter, ending 2.30 m south of Lake's own north platted kerb. The owner's ruling anticipated a collision and named T-0251 to settle it — the loser re-seated on its own evidence before it is withdrawn — and this line's own evidence is the rule above. The cost is written where the street is, in data/streets/1835.json: Fergus 1839's 'W. Water st north of West Lake st' again attests a street this reconstruction gives no modelled length north of Lake. Nothing already placed was displaced; the nearest committed footprint is James Kinzie's house, whose nearest corner stands 9.14 m north-west of this one.

AND THE PLATE'S COMPOSITION NOW READS, which is what T-0122 asked for and what the old placement could not give. Plate "11" of the 2026-08-11 prefire views hangs ship masts over this tavern's roofline; from the old stand the nearest water on that bearing was 157 m out and a 14.5 m mast on a 1.1 m deck needed to be inside 83 m, so the masts read beside and beyond the inn instead. The schooner moored in the reach below the forks (data/boats/era_boats.json, boat_schooner_wolf_point_2, whose own note already called this reach 'the one open water on the Green Tree Tavern's own eastward sight line') now lies 29.16 m beyond the ridge. The ridge stands 7.98 m above the building's base — 5.0 m of wall and a 38 degree gable over a 7.62 m width — which is 8.96 m on the committed heightfield, and the masthead is 15.6 m above the water. A viewer has to stand at least 0.93 of the ridge-to-mast distance back from the ridge before the masthead clears it, so the `green_tree` stand moved with the building, to Lake Street's own south platted frontage 34.85 m from the ridge on the schooner's bearing (local [-44.11, -121.52], yaw 33.3). The masthead reads 1.44 m above the roofline there, and between 1.36 m and 1.52 m for an eye anywhere from 1.6 m to 1.8 m. From the old standoff — 12.2 m off the front wall — it still does not clear, and that is geometry rather than a placement question: an 8 m ridge seen from 12 m subtends more than a 15.6 m masthead seen from 41 m, wherever the building stands.

placement.position_note: PLACED 2026-08-11. THE CORNER IS DOCUMENTED AND THE COORDINATE IS DERIVED, so the tag follows the weaker half. Andreas puts the log jail on 'the northwest corner of the court-house square'. The public square is the block bounded by Randolph Street on the north, Washington Street on the south, Clark Street on the east and LaSalle Street on the west - the block this project's own ground control identifies as such in data/traces/gcp/wright_1834_gcps.json, where LaSalle and Randolph is labelled 'NW corner of the Public Square block' and Clark and Washington 'SE corner of the Public Square block'. Its four inside corners were computed for this parcel from modern OpenStreetMap intersection centres fetched 2026-08-11, offset 12.2 m into the block on each axis, half of an 80 ft street per Hathaway 1834: NW 447538.25 / 4637130.78, NE 447639.27 / 4637130.25, SW 447541.20 / 4637018.49, SE 447639.80 / 4637018.05, which makes the block about 101 x 112 m. The jail's own north-west corner is set on the square's north-west corner, so the footprint origin - which is the building's south-west corner - sits its own depth south of it. THIS IS A CORNER OF A BLOCK, NOT A LOT, so it is a weaker statement than the corner-lot placements elsewhere in this dataset: nothing says how far into the block the building stood, whether it was set back from either street line, or which way it faced. WORKING UNCERTAINTY ABOUT 20 M from the georeference (data/datum.json: 17.5 m RMS on Wright 1834, 3.7 per cent paper stretch), plus an unquantified setback into the block. Facade bearing 0, due north onto Randolph, CONVENTION RATHER THAN EVIDENCE - a jail at the north-west corner could as reasonably have faced west onto LaSalle or inward onto the square, and nothing attests it. The square itself in 1835 was otherwise an open, unimproved prairie block, fenced or not; no fence, path or improvement of the block is modelled. RECONCILED WITH THE COMMITTED PLAT 2026-08-28 (T-0246), AND THE CLAIM DID NOT MOVE - ONLY THE LINE IT WAS DERIVED AGAINST. The method above found the square's north-west corner by taking modern OpenStreetMap intersection centres, fetched 2026-08-11, and stepping 12.2 m into the block on each axis. That is not this project's own Randolph Street: the committed centreline in data/streets/1835.json, offset by half the committed 80 ft corridor, is what tools/generate_plat_lots.py builds every platted block edge from, and it is the line every derived layer in this scene reads. Measured against it with tools/measure_corridor_intrusion.py, this footprint's north wall stood 3.48 m OUT PAST blk_randolph_lasalle's Randolph frontage line, in the platted roadway, with its centroid inside the corridor - deeper than any of the four Lake Street records T-0196 looked at - and tools/generate_frontage_works.py refused two steps of Randolph's plank walk, 0.0 to 10.4 m along that face, naming this building in the refusal. THE REPAIR IS THIS RECORD'S OWN METHOD RUN AGAINST THIS PROJECT'S OWN LINE: the footprint is translated 4.981 m along the face's inward normal - dE -0.040 m, dN -4.981 m in local ENU, so UTM E 447538.25 N 4637126.21 becomes E 447538.21 N 4637121.23 - which leaves its north wall 1.50 m back from the committed frontage line. THE SQUARE IS NOT SUBDIVIDED, so there is no lot line to stand off: 1.50 m is plat_occupancy.LOT_MARGIN_M, the plat module's own margin off a boundary, and it is the same figure the reconciled South Water and Lake records took off their lot lines (T-0127, T-0198, T-0199). NOTHING ALONG THE STREET MOVED: the along-face position, the block, the corner and the side are untouched, and so is the confidence grade - re-deriving a coordinate from better geometry is not new evidence, and Andreas's 'northwest corner of the court-house square' is what it always was. WHAT THIS DOES NOT REPAIR: the 20 m working uncertainty stated above is unchanged and dwarfs this 4.98 m, so the move is a reconciliation between two of this project's own lines and not a claim to have located the jail better. The facade bearing stays 0 while this face runs at 0.46 degrees, which leaves the front wall between 1.50 and 1.55 m back across its width; that skew is not corrected here, because rotating a record is a second claim and this one is a repair. V4 ENCLOSURE/ACCESS RECONSTRUCTION 2026-10-30: the earlier exact northing was a chosen setback derived from the public-square street line, not an attested building coordinate. Andreas attests the northwest part of the square, not the exact setback. Move only 1.30 m south within the stated roughly20 m working uncertainty, retaining easting, bearing, core fabric, footprint, parcel and every committed street input. This finite R placement allows the existing1.80 m native doorway approach plus0.25 m to the continuous palisade axis atN-269.25 (0.16 m beyond a180 mm backing post), rather than preserving an invented centre gap that is absent from the1902 drawing. The exact1.30 m is an access/layout convention, not survey evidence or a measured pictorial distance. The1836-captioned plate does not establish the July1835 arrangement; continuity remains R. The earlier placement and plat-reconciliation history above is retained as history, not a claim that the later R setback is derived.

liberty.text:
Partial lower-wall siding on the Agency House
DECISION
represent McKee’s account, quoted by Andreas, that the agency house was “afterward clapboarded part way up.” The existing five-room compound receives a lower band of neutral horizontal boards, with upper logs and notched ends exposed. No new paint, wall, roof, opening or site is claimed. The 1.30 m height is half the current inferred 2.6 m model wall, not a historical measurement. The inherited 0.14 m lap rhythm, 18 mm butt projection, chosen clearance from the log/chink skin and 0.246 m clearance at the ends of exposed runs are liberties. Leaving the existing notched corners and narrow junction strips unboarded avoids inventing concealed corner trim. Boards cover only the exterior union boundary and are cut around every current front opening. Existing dark faces, casings, roof forms and stacks remain in place. “Afterward” follows the account’s 1823 setting but supplies no completion date. Showing this finish in July1835 is reconstructed continuity, not a new dated finding. The unsolved panorama camera and the compound width, wings, sub-roofs, junctions, finish/tonal interpretation and whole-picture acceptance remain unresolved.
HOW TO RESOLVE
a dated account or legible elevation showing the height and extent of the siding would replace the chosen band and corner treatment.
SOURCES
Andreas, A. T. History of Chicago: From the Earliest Period to the Present Time, quoting McKee’s recollection; the existing Kinzie, Juliette A. M. Wau-Bun: The 'Early Day' in the North-West compound description remains controlling for composition.

corePlacement.position_note: PLACED 2026-08-11. THE CORNER IS DOCUMENTED AND THE COORDINATE IS DERIVED, so the tag follows the weaker half. Andreas puts the log jail on 'the northwest corner of the court-house square'. The public square is the block bounded by Randolph Street on the north, Washington Street on the south, Clark Street on the east and LaSalle Street on the west - the block this project's own ground control identifies as such in data/traces/gcp/wright_1834_gcps.json, where LaSalle and Randolph is labelled 'NW corner of the Public Square block' and Clark and Washington 'SE corner of the Public Square block'. Its four inside corners were computed for this parcel from modern OpenStreetMap intersection centres fetched 2026-08-11, offset 12.2 m into the block on each axis, half of an 80 ft street per Hathaway 1834: NW 447538.25 / 4637130.78, NE 447639.27 / 4637130.25, SW 447541.20 / 4637018.49, SE 447639.80 / 4637018.05, which makes the block about 101 x 112 m. The jail's own north-west corner is set on the square's north-west corner, so the footprint origin - which is the building's south-west corner - sits its own depth south of it. THIS IS A CORNER OF A BLOCK, NOT A LOT, so it is a weaker statement than the corner-lot placements elsewhere in this dataset: nothing says how far into the block the building stood, whether it was set back from either street line, or which way it faced. WORKING UNCERTAINTY ABOUT 20 M from the georeference (data/datum.json: 17.5 m RMS on Wright 1834, 3.7 per cent paper stretch), plus an unquantified setback into the block. Facade bearing 0, due north onto Randolph, CONVENTION RATHER THAN EVIDENCE - a jail at the north-west corner could as reasonably have faced west onto LaSalle or inward onto the square, and nothing attests it. The square itself in 1835 was otherwise an open, unimproved prairie block, fenced or not; no fence, path or improvement of the block is modelled. RECONCILED WITH THE COMMITTED PLAT 2026-08-28 (T-0246), AND THE CLAIM DID NOT MOVE - ONLY THE LINE IT WAS DERIVED AGAINST. The method above found the square's north-west corner by taking modern OpenStreetMap intersection centres, fetched 2026-08-11, and stepping 12.2 m into the block on each axis. That is not this project's own Randolph Street: the committed centreline in data/streets/1835.json, offset by half the committed 80 ft corridor, is what tools/generate_plat_lots.py builds every platted block edge from, and it is the line every derived layer in this scene reads. Measured against it with tools/measure_corridor_intrusion.py, this footprint's north wall stood 3.48 m OUT PAST blk_randolph_lasalle's Randolph frontage line, in the platted roadway, with its centroid inside the corridor - deeper than any of the four Lake Street records T-0196 looked at - and tools/generate_frontage_works.py refused two steps of Randolph's plank walk, 0.0 to 10.4 m along that face, naming this building in the refusal. THE REPAIR IS THIS RECORD'S OWN METHOD RUN AGAINST THIS PROJECT'S OWN LINE: the footprint is translated 4.981 m along the face's inward normal - dE -0.040 m, dN -4.981 m in local ENU, so UTM E 447538.25 N 4637126.21 becomes E 447538.21 N 4637121.23 - which leaves its north wall 1.50 m back from the committed frontage line. THE SQUARE IS NOT SUBDIVIDED, so there is no lot line to stand off: 1.50 m is plat_occupancy.LOT_MARGIN_M, the plat module's own margin off a boundary, and it is the same figure the reconciled South Water and Lake records took off their lot lines (T-0127, T-0198, T-0199). NOTHING ALONG THE STREET MOVED: the along-face position, the block, the corner and the side are untouched, and so is the confidence grade - re-deriving a coordinate from better geometry is not new evidence, and Andreas's 'northwest corner of the court-house square' is what it always was. WHAT THIS DOES NOT REPAIR: the 20 m working uncertainty stated above is unchanged and dwarfs this 4.98 m, so the move is a reconciliation between two of this project's own lines and not a claim to have located the jail better. The facade bearing stays 0 while this face runs at 0.46 degrees, which leaves the front wall between 1.50 and 1.55 m back across its width; that skew is not corrected here, because rotating a record is a second claim and this one is a repair. V4 ENCLOSURE/ACCESS RECONSTRUCTION 2026-10-30: the earlier exact northing was a chosen setback derived from the public-square street line, not an attested building coordinate. Andreas attests the northwest part of the square, not the exact setback. Move only 1.30 m south within the stated roughly20 m working uncertainty, retaining easting, bearing, core fabric, footprint, parcel and every committed street input. This finite R placement allows the existing1.80 m native doorway approach plus0.25 m to the continuous palisade axis atN-269.25 (0.16 m beyond a180 mm backing post), rather than preserving an invented centre gap that is absent from the1902 drawing. The exact1.30 m is an access/layout convention, not survey evidence or a measured pictorial distance. The1836-captioned plate does not establish the July1835 arrangement; continuity remains R. The earlier placement and plat-reconciliation history above is retained as history, not a claim that the later R setback is derived.

placement.position_note: PLACED 2026-08-11. THE CORNER IS DOCUMENTED TWICE AND THE COORDINATE IS DERIVED, so the tag follows the weaker half — the rule the Sauganash and Green Tree placements use. Wau-Bun: 'It stood at what is now the southwest corner of Wolcott and N. Water Streets.' Andreas, independently: 'the agency-house on the north side of the river, near where now is the foot of North State Street', with his footnote citing Wau-Bun for the same corner. METHOD, in three steps. (1) Wolcott Street is today's N State Street; its modern centreline was read from OpenStreetMap through the Kinzie intersection (EPSG:26916 E 447899.73, N 4637671.53, local E +827.0, N +275.7) and carried south on the fitted bearing of the OSM centreline, giving E +830 at this northing and a west kerb 12.2 m west of it, half an 80 ft platted street. (2) North Water Street and the 1834 north bank were read off the Wright 1834 sheet at the project's own fitted affine (tools/wright_px.py, the same transform tools/rederive_datum.py checks the datum against): the north-bank block row's south line, which is North Water Street's north kerb, runs at local N +128 to +132 between E +624 and E +812, and the drawn north bank of the main stem runs at local N +98 over the same stretch. So the platted street occupies a strip about 30 m deep between the block row and the water. (3) The building's south face is set 15 m north of that bank line and its east face 4 m west of the State Street kerb. THE 15 M IS EVIDENCE, NOT A GUESS, AND IT IS SOFT: Andreas prints the testimony of Charles Jouett's daughter, Mrs. Susan M. Callis, who came here in 1816 and describes the agency house of that period as 'a log building of two large rooms, about twenty steps from the river bank, on the north side'. Twenty steps is 15-18 m. Two inferences ride on it — that a step is about three-quarters of a metre, and that the house Mrs. Callis describes is the one Wolcott finished, which Andreas's 'commenced during Judge Jouett's incumbency' supports and nobody states. WHAT THE SOUTH-WEST QUADRANT ACTUALLY IS: on the 1834 sheet there is no block in it. West of Wolcott the ground south of North Water Street is the riverbank itself, so the building sits on the bank between the platted street and the water rather than on a corner lot — which is what Wau-Bun describes from the other side: 'when, in the process of the town's improvement, a street was maliciously opened directly in the rear of the building, the whole establishment, with its comical little adjuncts, was a constant source of amusement to the passers-by.' The house predates the plat by a decade and the street was laid out behind it. That same sentence is the evidence for the facade bearing recorded here, 180, due south onto the river: the street opened at the REAR, so the front faced the water, which is also how the fort's people reached it — Wau-Bun has the intercourse between the garrison and the Agency House kept up by canoe. UNCERTAINTY: about 20 m from the georeference (data/datum.json records ~17.5 m RMS and calls 20 m the working figure), plus the reading of the 1834 sheet by eye at about 5 m, plus whatever 'twenty steps' is worth. Treat the across-bank axis as the softer one. A LARGER CAVEAT THAN ALL OF THOSE, AND IT IS DISCHARGED. When this note was written the building stood about 500 m east of the modelled terrain box and there was no modelled ground under it at all. The e1834_harbor_cut heightfield was extended east on 2026-08-11 to local E -320..+1700, N -400..+400 — docs/LIBERTIES.md L17 is revised to say so — and this position has stood on traced ground at about +1.35 m above the summer-1835 water surface ever since, which is why this phase carries no ground_contact declaration. Corrected 2026-08-22 under T-0010; walked in the real page by tools/measure_east_band.mjs.

footprint.note: PLACEHOLDER. THE SHAPE CARRIES EVIDENCE AND EVERY NUMBER IN IT IS INVENTED, and the two must not be confused — the same distinction miller_house's footprint note draws. What is attested is the composition, from the only description of this building anybody wrote: 'a substantial, compact little building of logs hewed and squared, with a centre, two wings, and, strictly speaking, two tails, since, when there was found no more room for additions at the sides, they were placed in the rear, whereon a vacant spot could be found. These appendages did not mar the symmetry of the whole, as viewed from the front.' This polygon is that sentence drawn: a centre block projecting one metre forward of two flanking wings, so the front reads symmetrical, and two tails running back from the rear of the centre. The dimensions — a 5 m centre, 4 m wings, 1.5 m tails, a 13 x 9 m envelope — are chosen to suit the words 'compact little building' and are supported by nothing. Mrs. Callis's 'two large rooms' describes the house in 1816, before the wings and tails, and is the only interior evidence of any kind. NOTE WHAT THE MESH DOES WITH THIS: the log_dwelling archetype masses the polygon's BOUNDING BOX, so the visitor sees a plain 13 x 9 m rectangle and the composition this polygon draws is not built — the re-entrant corners beside the tails and beside the wings are filled in. That is admitted in docs/LIBERTIES.md rather than hidden, and it is the same limitation L27 records for Miller's house. To resolve: any plan, any dimension, or the Chicago Democrat's advertisements for the agency's buildings. T-2374 SUPERSESSION: the opt-in the connected room layout now builds five rooms whose union is this polygon, rather than its bounding box. The preceding paragraph describes the prior mesh limitation; its dimension and date cautions still apply.

construction.note: Wau-Bun: 'a substantial, compact little building of logs hewed and squared'. Andreas, recording David McKee's account of the north side when he arrived in 1823: 'All these houses were of logs — the agency-house being afterward clapboarded part way up.' Hewn and squared log is exactly what this archetype builds. The clapboarding is recorded separately under `cladding`, with its unknown extent and date kept explicit there.

cladding.note: 'the agency-house being afterward clapboarded part way up' — David McKee's recollection, printed by Andreas. This is an unusually specific finish for a building at this date and it is genuinely odd: siding taken part of the way up a log wall and no further, presumably to weather the lower courses. WHEN it was done is not stated beyond 'afterward', i.e. after 1823, so whether the boards were there on the scene date is not attested either. T-2374: the lower-wall trial now represents this occurrence through compound_clapboard_height_m; its chosen half-wall extent, neutral finish and corner clearances are liberties; the original date qualification remains.

plan_composition.value: centre, two wings, two rear tails
plan_composition.note: Wau-Bun's phrase, kept verbatim as a value because it is the single best-attested fact about this building and because the footprint polygon that draws it is not what the mesh is built from. The record states the composition; the model shows a rectangle. T-2374: the centre, wings and tails are now represented by the connected room layout; the preceding rectangle limitation is historical. Their exact arrangement and intersecting gables remain reconstructed.

stories.note: Not attested. 'Compact little building' and 'two large rooms' both read as a single storey, and a building that grew by adding wings at the sides and tails at the rear is a building that could not grow upward — which is the argument. The counter-example is in the same book: the FIRST agency house, built beside old Fort Dearborn in 1803-4 on the south side, was 'a two-story log building, covered with split oak siding'. That is a different building and it is why this value is inference rather than type.

wall_height_m.note: No figure is attested. 2.6 m is about 8 ft 6 in: one storey of hewn-log wall at the course counts this project uses for the Miller house's log core, plus a sill. What is inferred is the range, not the centimetre.

roof_type.note: THE ONE THING WAU-BUN SAYS ABOUT THIS ROOF IS THAT IT WAS NOT ORDINARY: 'There were pleasant, happy hours passed under its odd-shaped roof.' Odd-shaped is what a centre with two wings and two tails produces — a roof of intersecting ridges, valleys and lean-tos that grew with the additions. The archetype builds one gable over one rectangle, so the model shows the opposite of what the source says, and the value is tagged conjectural because a gable here is a substitution rather than a reading. Left as `gable` rather than `shed` because a gable is the only one of the two forms this archetype offers that a log building of this size would carry. T-2374: the connected room layout replaces the former single gable with intersecting gables; no elevation establishes that this reconstructed roof matches the odd-shaped original.

roof_pitch_deg.note: No pitch is attested. 35 degrees is this archetype's mid-range for a low log building roofed in riven shakes. Inferred from construction practice, not measured, and inherited by a roof form the record has already said is wrong (see roof_type). T-2374 retains this pitch for each reconstructed compound roof.

chimneys.note: Not attested. Two is inferred from the plan the sources give rather than from the building: a centre with two wings, holding the agent's office and household — in 1831 that household was J. H. Kinzie's mother, two sisters and brother as well — is more rooms than one hearth heats through a Chicago winter. The COUNT is the inference; where the stacks stand, how big they are and what they are made of are the archetype's, which is the standing admission in docs/LIBERTIES.md L26. T-2374 retains the inferred count but chooses the outer wing gable ends, with reconstructed positions and inherited sections, rather than the former bbox gable ends.

compound_parts.note: T-2374 first massing increment: Wau-Bun's centre, two wings and two rear tails now become five connected log rooms. Wall rectangles exactly partition the already reconstructed footprint; every dimension remains invented. Wing roofs extend to the centre ridge to conceal internal gable ends, giving intersecting roof planes. All five eaves inherit the inferred 2.6 m wall height. Roof directions, extensions, junctions, one central front door, one window on each wing, and both outer-wing stack positions are reconstructed, not read from the small retrospective panorama. No pictured opening count, roof pitch, valley detail, finish or 1835 continuation is established. This does not settle the agency-house identification in the panorama or constitute an image match. See L-cobweb-compound-2374.

compound_apertures.note: T-2374 FRONT APERTURE INCREMENT, AND THE COUNT IS THE ONLY THING THE PICTURE GIVES. The keyed panorama 'Fort Dearborn and Chicago in 1831', read here at full resolution on its Agency-House subject (chicago/reference/images/chicago/chicago_fort_dearborn_1831_1.jpg, sha256 624d8f1f52a75bf30653e8cbf37a388478b0ddf5a02f1fadf727cf2144b84c3f), draws the front gable with THREE dark marks: TWO upright ones standing on the ground line, and ONE small one high on the face at the head of the wall. The archetype's compound path states one opening per room, so that front could not be expressed at all and every data-only attempt at it was refused by the archetype's own validation; this attribute is the opt-in that lets one room state its own set, and it OVERRIDES the centre door that room's `front_opening` would otherwise put here, so the old opening does not survive among the new marks. WHAT IS READ AND WHAT IS INVENTED. Read from the picture: that there are two lower marks and one upper one; that the lower pair stand on the ground; and roughly where the three fall along the face, the lower pair in its left and middle leaving the right-hand stretch blank, the upper mark a little left of the apex. Invented: every dimension, every band, the depth and section of the recesses, and which of the two lower marks is the way in. The marks are a few pixels across a thirty-pixel gable in a retrospective engraving whose proportions are not this model's, so no fraction of them is carried across as a measurement: the coordinates here are set out from this record's own 5 m central wall and the rake of its own roof, inside the bounds the archetype validates. The face is drawn slightly oblique, which compresses its right-hand side, so even the arrangement is read with that caution. THE ENTRY ROLE IS A DESIGN INFERENCE AND NOT A READING. The picture does not say which mark was a door, or that either was. The right-hand one carries `kind: door` because it stands where this record's previous single centre door stood, so the town's entrance, apron and doorway clearance keep the ground they already held; the other is `kind: aperture`, which claims a hole and nothing else. No glazing, closure, interior, attic room, white paint or historic function is claimed by any of the three, and the white of the engraving's paper is not evidence of paint. WHAT THIS DOES NOT SETTLE. The source is retrospective 1831 context printed in 1881, not proof of the building as it stood on 1835-07-01; the camera on it remains unsolved and is not enrolled in data/reference_views/. The compound's overall width, the wing and sub-roof silhouettes, the roof junctions, the text-attested partial clapboarding and the building's finish and tone are all unchanged and still open. T-2374's image gate stays open. See L-cobweb-apertures-2374.

Stack count, outer-wing positions, sections, roofs, occupied footprint and placement remain unchanged; T-2374's image gate remains open.

function.note: NOT AN OPERATING INDIAN AGENCY BUILDING AT THE SCENE DATE, most likely, and that is the fact this record has least evidence for. Hamilton, the county's clerk and commissioner of school lands, living in it as a private house while the agency's business ran down through the 1833 treaty. placement.position_note:
RE-SEATED 2026-10-22 ON THE OWNER'S REPORT (T-3029): 5.80 m WEST, the northing and bearing unchanged. The owner, in the 1835 scene: "green tree tavern in 1835 is sunken, it needs to be on the ground". It was: the renderer beds a building on the lowest ground under it, and the T-0141 seat below was measured on the footprint polygon alone, while the rear ell (form.rear_ell, built since T-0083 off the east gable) runs 4.5 m further down the bank, its far corner 1.54 m from the traced waterline. Bedded to the ell's foot, the inn stood 0.58 m under its own front door; bedded to its bounding box, as the renderer then did, 0.88 m. The rule is the T-0141 rule with the whole building in it: walked west a tenth of a metre at a time, this is the first seat at which every wall foot the mesh puts on the ground, ell included, meets the modelled ground within 0.10 m, the relief 95% of the 1835 town's structures stand on. Here it is 0.099 m, and the ell's far corner stands 4.59 m from the bank. The move is inside the 20 m working uncertainty below and argues nothing new about the corner: the source still puts the inn at Lake and West Water, and the bank still decides how close to it the inn can come. The paragraphs below are the T-0141 seat as it was measured, kept as the reading this one corrects.

MOVED 2026-09-24 ON THE OWNER'S RULING OF 2026-09-21 (T-0141): from the north-east corner of Lake and Canal to the north-east corner of Lake and West Water, 116.40 m east, measured between the old east face and the new one. The northing did not change at all. THE MOVE IS ARGUED FROM THE SOURCE AND NOT FROM A PICTURE'S FRAMING. DRLOIH's article on this tavern gives the corner as 'Lake and West Water Streets'; West Water was the street that ran along the west bank while Canal lay a full plat module further west, and the owner ruled that statement preferred over the same article's gloss 'now Canal Street'. The ship masts that read beside and beyond the inn rather than above its own roofline from the `green_tree` stand (T-0122, T-0140) are the SYMPTOM that sent somebody to look at the placement; they are not a reason to move a building.

WHAT THE OLD PLACEMENT WAS, because a committed building that moves without its previous reading surviving is a town quietly rewriting itself. PLACED 2026-08-09 at EPSG:26916 E 446937.4, N 4637299.6, facade bearing 270: the west face on Canal Street's east frontage and the south face on Lake's north frontage, each half an 80 ft platted street from the modern Lake-and-Canal intersection centre read from OpenStreetMap (E 446913.0, N 4637287.4). That reading rested on chicagology's 'Northeast Corner of Lake and Canal Streets' and on DRLOIH's own body text, 'the N.E. corner of what is now Lake and Canal Streets' — both name Canal in modern terms and one says 'what is now', which is why Canal was adopted at the time. The residual was recorded then and is the thing the ruling settled: modern Canal at Lake stands about 146 m back from the modern west-bank line, so the two readings are a full plat module apart. The check that would settle it from paper is still the lot geometry on Wright 1834 or Hathaway 1834, which nobody has read.

HOW THE NEW COORDINATE IS ARRIVED AT — two constraints, one of them recomputed by tools/validate.py. (1) NORTH OF LAKE, unchanged: the south face stands 12.192 m north of the Lake-and-Canal control's northing, half the 80 ft platted module, which is the `platted_corner` derivation below and keeps the building out of Lake's platted corridor. (2) THE RIVER END: the footprint's north-east corner stands 3.01 m from the 1834 traced west bank of the South Branch (data/terrain/epochs/e1834_harbor_cut/river.geojson) — 5.71 m measured due east at that corner's own northing — and the standoff is the MODELLED GROUND'S OWN LIMIT rather than a chosen setback. The bank falls away toward the water, and a 12.19 m sill plate cannot sit level across that fall: seated hard on the bank the footprint's perimeter stands 0.88 m off the terrain beneath it, which is a building arriving nowhere and would owe a liberty. Walked west a tenth of a metre at a time, the first seat whose whole perimeter comes within the walker's 0.35 m step-up of the modelled ground is this one, at 0.294 m, with the footprint dry at all 425 samples of a 24-by-16 grid over it. So the tavern comes forward to the bank as far as the committed ground carries it, which is what 'forward to the bank' can mean here. Facade bearing is UNCHANGED at 270, due west onto West Water: F. H. Taylor's 'The fornt was on Canal street and this side was on Lake' is a claim about the street the front faced, and on the ruling's reading that street is West Water; the long elevation still runs east-west along Lake, and John Gray's second entrance is still 'on the Lake street front about the middle of the long side'. Working uncertainty about 20 m, which is the georeference's and the traced bank's and not an additional guess.

WHAT THE MOVE DISPLACED, AND ON WHOSE RULE. The committed `west_water` centreline ran through this footprint. T-0768 carried the bank offset 37.12 m past the Wolf Point turn under a stated rule — carry it until the riverward corridor reaches a committed footprint that stands ACROSS the roadway rather than beside it, and cut the line there — and the Green Tree is now the first such footprint, its nearest corner 3.01 m from the bank and its furthest 15.90 m, so it stands across the roadway exactly as James Kinzie's house does. So the line is cut at local [-20.32, -98.49]: 22.53 m shorter, ending 2.30 m south of Lake's own north platted kerb. The owner's ruling anticipated a collision and named T-0251 to settle it — the loser re-seated on its own evidence before it is withdrawn — and this line's own evidence is the rule above. The cost is written where the street is, in data/streets/1835.json: Fergus 1839's 'W. Water st north of West Lake st' again attests a street this reconstruction gives no modelled length north of Lake. Nothing already placed was displaced; the nearest committed footprint is James Kinzie's house, whose nearest corner stands 9.14 m north-west of this one.

AND THE PLATE'S COMPOSITION NOW READS, which is what T-0122 asked for and what the old placement could not give. Plate "11" of the 2026-08-11 prefire views hangs ship masts over this tavern's roofline; from the old stand the nearest water on that bearing was 157 m out and a 14.5 m mast on a 1.1 m deck needed to be inside 83 m, so the masts read beside and beyond the inn instead. The schooner moored in the reach below the forks (data/boats/era_boats.json, boat_schooner_wolf_point_2, whose own note already called this reach 'the one open water on the Green Tree Tavern's own eastward sight line') now lies 29.16 m beyond the ridge. The ridge stands 7.98 m above the building's base — 5.0 m of wall and a 38 degree gable over a 7.62 m width — which is 8.96 m on the committed heightfield, and the masthead is 15.6 m above the water. A viewer has to stand at least 0.93 of the ridge-to-mast distance back from the ridge before the masthead clears it, so the `green_tree` stand moved with the building, to Lake Street's own south platted frontage 34.85 m from the ridge on the schooner's bearing (local [-44.11, -121.52], yaw 33.3). The masthead reads 1.44 m above the roofline there, and between 1.36 m and 1.52 m for an eye anywhere from 1.6 m to 1.8 m. From the old standoff — 12.2 m off the front wall — it still does not clear, and that is geometry rather than a placement question: an 8 m ridge seen from 12 m subtends more than a 15.6 m masthead seen from 41 m, wherever the building stands.
placement.symbolic_location: North-east corner of Lake Street and West Water Street, on the west bank of the South Branch; the long elevation on Lake, the front west onto West Water, the river end on the bank as far as the modelled ground carries it.

footprint.note:
DERIVED FROM THE ATTESTED INTERIOR, not invented and not measured. This is the only footprint in the parcel with a textual basis. The arithmetic, in the original units: guest chambers 'about 12x12' feet, so a depth of two 12 ft ranks plus board partitions gives about 25 ft = 7.62 m; a hall 'divided the house' with the entrance 'about the middle of the long side', so the length is two end blocks either side of a hall of about 8 ft, and each end block must hold a 12 ft room plus partitions, giving about 40 ft = 12.19 m. The bar-room occupied one whole end, which is consistent. WHAT IS ATTESTED IS THE MODULE, NOT THE COUNT: no source gives the building's overall length or width, and a plan with three rooms rather than two on one side would make it about 52 ft. Treat the length as plus or minus about 20 per cent and the depth as firmer. The polygon is the two-storey core only — the 'low one-story addition to the right, the same as on the left' that John Gray recalls is NOT included, because its size is unattested and its date is unknown. The c. 1859 photograph (chm_green_tree_1859) would settle the overall dimensions from the proportions of a known-height building; it has not been seen.

T-2376: this polygon remains the main block's dimension/coordinate reference. The separately reconstructed left connector and gabled range are described by form.enclosed_left_annex. Their exact resolved occupied polygons are carried separately to physical consumers; the open wagon bay is not silently filled by a bounding rectangle. This does not add an archival dimension or date to the core. This model-only preparation does not yet qualify additional occupied solids or navigation/ground consumers; the main-body footprint stays unchanged until the separate compound-consumer work is verified.

stories.note: 'a two-story frame building' (DRLOIH), and chicagology's witnesses use the second floor throughout — 'a stairway in this hall led to the second floor'.

construction.note: DISPUTED, AND THE DISPUTE HAS A NAME ATTACHED TO IT. Two sources call the Green Tree a two-storey frame building outright. Against that, chicagology's Town of Chicago page reports that W. H. Stow — the man who built the Western Hotel two blocks south — 'did claim that the Green Tree was originally of logs and it was not until years afterward that it was covered with weatherboarding and given the appearance of a frame building.' Frame is adopted because it is the reading of both detailed accounts and because the interior the witnesses describe is a framed interior: board partitions, a stair hall, whitewashed plank walls, chambers laid out on a 12 ft module. The log-core claim is one man's recollection, recorded second-hand, about a rival's house, and it is carried in this record as log_core so it is not lost. Braced versus balloon is separately unattested: balloon framing appeared in Chicago in 1832-33, so an 1833 building could be either, and braced_frame is the conservative reading for the earlier date.

log_core.note: Records the rejected reading so it stays visible. W. H. Stow claimed the Green Tree was originally of logs and weatherboarded only years later. Adopted as false for the reasons in the construction note; if it is true, the 1835 building is a weatherboarded log structure rather than a frame one, which changes the wall section but not the massing, the plan or the placement.

cladding.note: Not directly attested for this building. Clapboard is the standard cladding for a frame building of this type and period, and the competing log-core account calls the covering 'weatherboarding', which is the same thing under another name — so both readings of the construction converge on a lapped horizontal board exterior.

paint.note: A CORRECTION TO A CLAIM IN CIRCULATION. The Green Tree is sometimes described as whitewashed, including in this project's own research summary, but the attested whitewash is INTERIOR: Edwin Gale writes that 'The walls, ceilings, and board partitions had evidently received a coat of whitewash when the house was built'. Nothing describes the exterior finish. Unpainted weathered clapboard is the reading adopted, and it is positively supported by the Sauganash's white paint being remarkable at Wolf Point in 1831 — if the Green Tree had been painted white two years later, the contrast the sources draw would be weaker. Not attested either way; the c. 1859 photograph would settle it.

wall_height_m.note: THE BEST-FOUNDED WALL HEIGHT IN THE DATASET, because a ceiling height is actually attested: 'Seven and one-half feet is rather low for a hotel ceiling.' Two storeys at 7 1/2 ft = 15 ft, plus floor structure between them and a sill course, gives about 16 1/2 ft = 5.0 m to the plate. The 7 1/2 ft is documented; the allowance for joists and sill is the inference.

roof_type.note: John Gray: 'There should also be a small attic window in the gable end, for we used the attic, too.' A gable end with a window in it is a direct attestation of the roof form — one of the few in this dataset that is not typological. With the front on Canal and the long side on Lake, the gable ends face east and west and the ridge runs east-west along Lake Street.

roof_pitch_deg.note: No pitch is attested. 38 degrees is mid-range for period gable framing and leaves an attic tall enough to lodge people in, which the sources say it did.

fenestration.note: The PANE CHARACTER is attested — a guest chamber 'about 12x12, with two windows 6x8', small-paned sash, plus 'a small attic window in the gable end'. Two windows per 12 ft chamber on a 40 x 25 ft two-storey block implies a regularly fenestrated elevation. Since T-0083 the ARRANGEMENT is carried by elevation_scheme, read off plate '11'; this value still states the pane character, which the plate agrees with — 6-over-6 sash in even bays.

elevation_scheme.note: THE BUILDING FRONTS ON A GABLE END, AND ITS EVEN BAYS RUN ALONG THE EAVES ELEVATIONS. Two halves, separately grounded. That the front is a gable end is a join of attested facts already in this record: the front on Canal (F. H. Taylor), the long side on Lake, and the gable ends facing east and west (John Gray's attic window note, and the roof_type note's own reading). The bay ARRANGEMENT — even 6-over-6 sash in regular bays along the long elevation, doors and attic lights on the gable faces — is read off plate '11' of the owner's 2026-08-11 reference set, committed at data/sources/assets/prefire_views_kevin_2026_08/p6_0.png: a tier-5 retrospective view, which may drive fenestration rhythm as inferred and may never drive a coordinate. The plate is not yet held as a source record (T-0075 owns that), so the citation is a committed path. The pictured south eaves elevation's bay count is now stated separately by eaves_bays on T-2376; the opposite elevation keeps the archetype's footprint arithmetic as a reconstruction under docs/LIBERTIES.md L152. No dimension or geographic placement is taken from the plate.

side_entrance.note: PICTURE-LED SOUTH EAVES OPENING PATTERN FOR THE 1835 MODEL, not a finding that this inn never had a side door. The held Andreas/Braunhold reproduction shows seven sash on the south long elevation on each floor, with a sash at the middle ground-floor station. The independently held original Trowbridge plate in Gale 1902, facing p.35 / scan n55, captioned 'The Green Tree Tavern in 1835', shows the same seven-bay window rhythm and no middle ground-floor door; its frontmost lower sash is partly obscured by the hanging board and people, while the middle station is visible. Setting this existing attribute to null selects the archetype's normal sash at all seven existing south-wall stations instead of substituting a door at the fourth station. The earlier John Gray testimony is retained here verbatim: 'on the Lake street front about the middle of the long side', with the hall and stairway behind it (chicagology_prefire127, transcribing the Inter Ocean, 1 July 1883; Gray kept the inn in 1838-41). That later recollection may describe a changed or schematic form, but it does not date the door to 1 July 1835, and the drawings do not prove its historical absence on that date. The choice follows the two pictured opening patterns as inferred form; exact July-1835 appearance remains uncertain. The original undated Andreas plate is not dated by the local reproduction's 1838 caption, and Trowbridge is retrospective, not an independent contemporary 1835 survey. Existing south-wall seven-bay count, even spacing, stock sash dimensions and height bands, north-wall rhythm, primary front entrance, footprint, geographic placement and all other form values stay unchanged. No c.1859 check_required photograph or Gray-derived new geometry supplies this correction; the two public-domain picture records supply the visible sash pattern.

chimney_placement.note: END CHIMNEYS AT BOTH GABLES. Plate '11' of the owner's 2026-08-11 reference set (committed at data/sources/assets/prefire_views_kevin_2026_08/p6_0.png, and its sibling Braunhold view written up as image 6 of data/sources/assets/owner_brief_2026_08_18/README.md) draws one stack at each end of the ridge — a tier-5 retrospective view driving massing as inferred. The plates are not yet held as source records (T-0075), so the citation is a committed path. This replaces the archetype's frontage-fraction arrangement, which on this deeper-than-wide footprint had left both stacks standing OFF the ridge on the roof slopes — the before frame of T-0083 shows it. The COUNT stays the chimneys attribute's own inference; docs/LIBERTIES.md L21 (the town chimney arrangement) and L152 say what is invented here.

rear_ell.note:
T-2376 retires the old rear ell as a July-1835 depiction choice. Its original position was a reconstruction made under the obsolete Canal placement, using the pictured lower wing and Gray's later testimony without a dated rear plan. The governing drawings do not resolve or show that projecting right/rear form. Gray explicitly recalls a right addition 'the same as on the left' during his 1838–41 tenancy, and the historical note promised a second wing if the Lake-and-West-Water placement won; that later bilateral testimony and the promise remain counterevidence, not proof that either addition was absent in 1835 or that both were the same pictured building. The revised model builds the pictured left connector/range, keeps the competing shoulder readings, and leaves an unverified 1835 rear/bilateral stage unmodeled rather than presenting the old placement proxy as another established wing. No historic absence, alteration date, tenant identity or room count is asserted.

HISTORICAL PRE-RETIREMENT NOTE:
THE LOW ADDITION, BUILT AT THE REAR AND DECLARED. John Gray, landlord 1838-41, attests 'a low one-story addition to the right, the same as on the left'; the 1838 Braunhold engraving (owner_brief_2026_08_18 README, image 6) draws 'a lower gabled wing at the left with a wide (carriage) door', and plate '11' (prefire_views_kevin_2026_08/p6_0.png) draws the low gabled wing with the ship masts behind it. WHETHER A WING STOOD ON 1835-07-01 IS NOT ATTESTED — Gray describes the house three to six years after the scene date — so this is a reconstruction under the owner's 2026-08-18 standing ruling, sized by the views and claimed at docs/LIBERTIES.md L152. WHY THE REAR END AND ONLY THE REAR: Gray names additions at BOTH ends, but this record's committed placement puts the west face ON Canal Street's east frontage with zero offset, so the street end has no ground to build on — only the east (rear, yard) end does. That asymmetry is itself evidence worth recording: a west wing fits the ground only under the 'Lake and West Water' placement reading the position note carries as this record's largest residual uncertainty. If that reading ever wins, the second wing goes up with the move. The wing the views draw beside masts is consistent with either.

gallery.note: NO EVIDENCE EITHER WAY, and unlike the Sauganash there is no retrospective depiction in the project's hands to reason from. The witnesses describe two entrances — the front on Canal and one 'about the middle of the long side' on Lake — without mentioning a porch, veranda or gallery, which is weak negative evidence at best, since they were correcting a drawing rather than inventorying the elevation. False is the default, not a finding. The c. 1859 photograph (chm_green_tree_1859) settles this the moment anyone opens it.

side_additions.note: John Gray, landlord 1838-41, correcting a drawing of the house: 'There should also be a low one-story addition to the right, the same as on the left.' So by the end of the 1830s the two-storey core had a low single-storey addition at each end. WHETHER THEY EXISTED ON 1835-07-01 IS NOT ATTESTED — Gray's testimony describes the building three to six years after the scene date — which is why this is inferred and why the additions stay out of the footprint polygon. SINCE T-0083 the rear (east) one is BUILT, at the reconstructed tier, as form.rear_ell — see that attribute for why only the rear end has ground to build on. This value stays the testimony record for BOTH ends; the street-end addition remains unbuilt.

chimneys.note: Not attested in text. A tavern with a bar-room at one end, a parlour, a dining room clearable for dancing and chambers above needed more than one fireplace, and two stacks is the normal disposition for a 40 ft block with a central hall. The number is inference — and since T-0083 it agrees with plate '11', which draws exactly two. WHERE they stand is carried by chimney_placement.

siding_exposure_m.note: INVENTED WITHIN A STOCK SET, NOT DERIVED. No source states the exposed face of any Chicago building's siding. The value is one of four period mill sidings — 4.5, 5, 5.5 or 6 in to the weather; this record wears 5 in — dealt by tools/deal_siding_stock.py: keyed to the phase's construction season, because buildings sided from the same season's shipments of St Joseph sawn lumber tend toward one stock, then advanced so no frame building within 60 m shares this one's. The separation is the surface variety T-0049 reconstructs, not a claim about 1835. docs/LIBERTIES.md L148 owns the invention.

front_ground_layout.note: Two sash left of a rightmost front-gable entrance agree in the actually viewed Andreas 1884 p634/n1301 plate, Trowbridge/Gale 1902 plate facing p35/n55, and Kurz & Allison 1893 panel11. This is retrospective form agreement, not independent contemporaneous proof of 1 July 1835; Kurz may derive from Andreas and Trowbridge may rely on later material. placement.position_note: PLACED 2026-08-11. THE CORNER IS DOCUMENTED AND THE COORDINATE IS DERIVED, so the tag follows the weaker half. Andreas puts the log jail on 'the northwest corner of the court-house square'. The public square is the block bounded by Randolph Street on the north, Washington Street on the south, Clark Street on the east and LaSalle Street on the west - the block this project's own ground control identifies as such in data/traces/gcp/wright_1834_gcps.json, where LaSalle and Randolph is labelled 'NW corner of the Public Square block' and Clark and Washington 'SE corner of the Public Square block'. Its four inside corners were computed for this parcel from modern OpenStreetMap intersection centres fetched 2026-08-11, offset 12.2 m into the block on each axis, half of an 80 ft street per Hathaway 1834: NW 447538.25 / 4637130.78, NE 447639.27 / 4637130.25, SW 447541.20 / 4637018.49, SE 447639.80 / 4637018.05, which makes the block about 101 x 112 m. The jail's own north-west corner is set on the square's north-west corner, so the footprint origin - which is the building's south-west corner - sits its own depth south of it. THIS IS A CORNER OF A BLOCK, NOT A LOT, so it is a weaker statement than the corner-lot placements elsewhere in this dataset: nothing says how far into the block the building stood, whether it was set back from either street line, or which way it faced. WORKING UNCERTAINTY ABOUT 20 M from the georeference (data/datum.json: 17.5 m RMS on Wright 1834, 3.7 per cent paper stretch), plus an unquantified setback into the block. Facade bearing 0, due north onto Randolph, CONVENTION RATHER THAN EVIDENCE - a jail at the north-west corner could as reasonably have faced west onto LaSalle or inward onto the square, and nothing attests it. The square itself in 1835 was otherwise an open, unimproved prairie block, fenced or not; no fence, path or improvement of the block is modelled. RECONCILED WITH THE COMMITTED PLAT 2026-08-28 (T-0246), AND THE CLAIM DID NOT MOVE - ONLY THE LINE IT WAS DERIVED AGAINST. The method above found the square's north-west corner by taking modern OpenStreetMap intersection centres, fetched 2026-08-11, and stepping 12.2 m into the block on each axis. That is not this project's own Randolph Street: the committed centreline in data/streets/1835.json, offset by half the committed 80 ft corridor, is what tools/generate_plat_lots.py builds every platted block edge from, and it is the line every derived layer in this scene reads. Measured against it with tools/measure_corridor_intrusion.py, this footprint's north wall stood 3.48 m OUT PAST blk_randolph_lasalle's Randolph frontage line, in the platted roadway, with its centroid inside the corridor - deeper than any of the four Lake Street records T-0196 looked at - and tools/generate_frontage_works.py refused two steps of Randolph's plank walk, 0.0 to 10.4 m along that face, naming this building in the refusal. THE REPAIR IS THIS RECORD'S OWN METHOD RUN AGAINST THIS PROJECT'S OWN LINE: the footprint is translated 4.981 m along the face's inward normal - dE -0.040 m, dN -4.981 m in local ENU, so UTM E 447538.25 N 4637126.21 becomes E 447538.21 N 4637121.23 - which leaves its north wall 1.50 m back from the committed frontage line. THE SQUARE IS NOT SUBDIVIDED, so there is no lot line to stand off: 1.50 m is plat_occupancy.LOT_MARGIN_M, the plat module's own margin off a boundary, and it is the same figure the reconciled South Water and Lake records took off their lot lines (T-0127, T-0198, T-0199). NOTHING ALONG THE STREET MOVED: the along-face position, the block, the corner and the side are untouched, and so is the confidence grade - re-deriving a coordinate from better geometry is not new evidence, and Andreas's 'northwest corner of the court-house square' is what it always was. WHAT THIS DOES NOT REPAIR: the 20 m working uncertainty stated above is unchanged and dwarfs this 4.98 m, so the move is a reconciliation between two of this project's own lines and not a claim to have located the jail better. The facade bearing stays 0 while this face runs at 0.46 degrees, which leaves the front wall between 1.50 and 1.55 m back across its width; that skew is not corrected here, because rotating a record is a second claim and this one is a repair. footprint.note: INVENTED. NO SOURCE REACHED GIVES THIS BUILDING A DIMENSION, a plan, or a number of cells. 6.096 x 4.572 m is 20 x 15 ft, recorded converted with the original figures stated per data/datum.json's units rule. The only constraint the evidence offers is relative and it runs in both directions: the jail was built because something more metropolitan was required than the estray pen, so it is a more substantial thing than a stock pound; and it was itself superseded within a few years, so it was small. A 20 x 15 ft log box is a two-cell lock-up and is the smallest thing that answers both. Nothing else about the shape is a finding: the plain rectangle, the proportion and the scale are all this record's.

construction.note: The building is named a LOG jail in the only description this project has of it, which makes the material the single best-attested thing about it. THE PLATE NOW SETTLES THE SECOND HALF OF IT: the engraving of the first Cook County jail in the owner's 2026-08-18 brief (data/sources/assets/owner_brief_2026_08_18/README.md, image 1) draws squared timber laid horizontally — 'a low log jail — squared timber, near-flat roof' — which is hewn log in courses with notched corners, exactly what this archetype builds for this value (generators/common/logwork.py). Until 2026-08-21 this note said hewn-versus-round was unattested and the archetype's hewn wall was a convention standing where evidence should be; the plate is that evidence, at tier 5, for the FABRIC and not for any dimension. Whether the walls were single or doubled, and whether they were lined inside, nothing reached says. The plate is a TIER 5 PICTORIAL held here as the brief's written record rather than a committed binary — the images were supplied in-session and T-0075 owns identifying them against the Andreas plate numbering and creating the source record — so it is cited by path, the way this dataset's other brief-driven attributes are (green_tree_tavern chimneys, image 6). The value's own grade is unchanged: 'log' was attested by Andreas before the plate and still is.

roof_type.note: GABLE IS KEPT, AND THE PLATE IS WHY THE PITCH MOVED RATHER THAN THE FORM. The engraving of the first cook county jail in the owner's 2026-08-18 brief (data/sources/assets/owner_brief_2026_08_18/readme.md, image 1) draws a near-flat roof. That is a statement about PITCH — this record's roof_pitch_deg now carries it — and it is not a statement about whether the roof fell one way or two: the brief holds the plate as a written description, and 'near-flat' distinguishes neither. So the form stays what it was reasoned to on 2026-08-11, and the reasoning is unchanged: gable is the near-universal roof form for log construction of this type, period and region, and it is what this project's other log buildings carry. The archetype would default a building this shallow to a shed roof, which is a covering appropriate to a lean-to; a purpose-built county jail is stated as gabled rather than left to that default. Typological derivation, not a measurement — and a single-slope reading of the same plate would be a legitimate rival that nothing this project holds can settle.

roof_pitch_deg.note: 12 DEGREES, THE PLATE'S NEAR-FLAT ROOF INSTEAD OF THIS ARCHETYPE'S DEFAULT. Superseded 2026-08-21. The value was 32.0 — the outbuilding archetype's own gable default, kept deliberately on 2026-08-11 because nothing attested a pitch and a fresh guess would have looked like a finding. The engraving of the first cook county jail in the owner's 2026-08-18 brief (data/sources/assets/owner_brief_2026_08_18/readme.md, image 1) is that evidence, and it is about this particular building: 'a low log jail — squared timber, near-flat roof'. A convention loses to a picture of the thing itself, so the pitch comes down. 12 degrees is the reading of 'near-flat' at this building's scale — 0.49 m of rise over the 2.29 m half-span, a cap on a box rather than a cabin's gable, and the whole building 0.94 m lower to its ridge than it stood yesterday. NOT LOWER THAN THAT, and the floor is the covering: this archetype roofs an outbuilding in boards laid down the slope rather than shingles (generators/archetypes/outbuilding.py _roof_plane), and a lapped board roof weighted or nailed down is the frontier form that goes near-flat where a riven-shake field cannot — the archetype's own note puts shakes at about 18 degrees minimum. WHAT IS INFERRED IS THAT THE PITCH IS LOW, NOT THAT IT IS 12: no plate can be measured to a degree, and a tier-5 pictorial may drive form and never a dimension of the ground.

wall_height_m.note: No figure is attested. 2.66 m is about 8 ft 9 in to the plate: a man's standing height with a header over the door and a course or two above it, which is what a lock-up needs and no more. It is also, to the centimetre, what this archetype's own size-aware default computes for a 20 x 15 ft footprint, and it is kept deliberately. THE PLATE CORROBORATES THE DIRECTION AND DOES NOT REPLACE THE NUMBER: the engraving of the first Cook County jail in the owner's 2026-08-18 brief (data/sources/assets/owner_brief_2026_08_18/README.md, image 1) draws a low, squat building, which is what a 2.66 m wall under a near-flat roof already is, and moving the figure to match a picture that carries no scale would be inventing a measurement out of an impression. What is inferred is that the height falls in this range, not that it is exactly 2.66 m. The squatness the plate shows is carried by roof_pitch_deg, which is the attribute the plate can actually speak to.

door.note: Not attested. `door` in this archetype names what has to get through the opening rather than whether there was one. A jail takes a person through in hand and nothing else - no horse, no wagon - so the man-door class is the reading, and it is the only one whose 1.88 m clear height fits under this wall. Where the door stood, what it was made of, and whether it was barred or grated is not attested and is the archetype's default.

function.note: Purpose-built for confinement, and it is the building that ended the practice recorded on the estray_pen record - prisoners held in the stock pound for want of anywhere else. Cook County was organised in 1831 and the county's business was conducted in rented rooms; this is the first purpose-built county structure of any kind and it precedes the court-house on the same block by about two years.
